assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength idea (a trapping wavelength at which the light shift cancels for the clock transition) with narrow-line optical spectroscopy of many atoms at once. It has taken time keeping to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and opened relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a route to redefining the second. The idea is original, the impact is concrete and the precision physics rests on atomic structure that I know well.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the optical lattice clock and the magic-wavelength concept and demonstrated the early strontium work. Ye's group brought the clock to record systematic uncertainty and stability and developed the comb-linked comparisons. The two-person configuration looks natural. I recall other groups (for example Lemonde and Le Targat in Paris, and Lisdat and Sterr in Germany) that also contributed, but the supplied credit does not include them. Whether the proposal or the demonstrated performance deserves more weight is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Strong and independent confirmation exists across Strontium, ytterbium and other species in many national laboratories, with international clock comparisons. The interpretation is stable. Recognition seems timely given the redefinition of the second now under discussion, and the earlier prizes for the ion trap and the frequency comb make this a natural continuation.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes (comb, ion control) could be argued either way for novelty.
I cannot confirm the exact priority dates from memory.
The redefinition of the second is not yet decided, so the practical impact is still partly prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new platform in which correlated insulators, superconductivity and orbital magnetism appear in a tunable, clean system. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted flat bands at a magic angle, and the 2018 experiments showed the correlated and superconducting phases. This is a field of its own now, with moiré quantum matter widely studied.
assessment.attribution: The theoretical prediction (MacDonald with Bistritzer) and the first experimental demonstration (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators) are clearly separable. The credited list contains three names and a prize can hold at most three, but a fair configuration probably favours the prediction and the experiment, so I propose MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. Bistritzer's role as co-author of the key paper is real; the allocation between him and MacDonald is the unresolved point. Other experimental groups (for example Dean and Young on moiré devices, and Efetov) and other theorists contributed but are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and the field is expanding fast. Some microscopic questions (the origin of the superconductivity, the role of strain and disorder) are not settled, but the discovery itself is secure. It is on the early side, but the impact is already large.
uncertainties: Whether the pairing mechanism and the full phase diagram are understood well enough does not affect the discovery but affects how the citation would be worded.
Credit between the theory pair and the broader moiré community is not fully captured by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall state in graphene-like systems and its realisation in HgTe quantum wells launched topological insulators, a major conceptual and experimental development linking band topology, protected edge states and spin-orbit coupling. The Z2 classification is a lasting contribution.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original theoretical proposals and the Z2 invariant; Molenkamp's group delivered the experimental observation in HgTe, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which is not in the supplied list. That omission is a real attribution problem, since BHZ identified the HgTe route. Within the supplied names the three-person configuration is coherent, with theory (Kane, Mele) and experiment (Molenkamp). I would also need to weigh Zhang (deceased) and the three-dimensional work.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed, including 3D topological insulators and the quantum anomalous Hall effect. The concept is mature and widely used, so recognition is timely, though the overlap with the 2016 topological-phase prize is worth noting.
uncertainties: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not among the credited names, so a prize built from this entry leaves out a decisive contributor.
Overlap with B014, which adds Qi-Kun Xue for the anomalous Hall effect, means the two entries partly describe the same field.
Overlap in scope with the 2016 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between a superconducting qubit and a single microwave photon routine and gave the architecture for superconducting quantum processors, with dispersive readout and quantum-state control. As an atomic theorist I recognise it as the cavity-QED idea transferred to a solid-state system, giving large coupling strengths and engineering flexibility. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits strengthens the foundation but concerns a different discovery.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the first experimental realisation (Wallraff, Schoelkopf and collaborators) fit three names. Girvin is a coauthor of the proposal and is not credited here, and the Yale group credit is shared. The configuration I propose looks fair on the supplied credit but is not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced throughout the field and underpins current quantum-computing demonstrations. Mature, but proximity to the 2025 circuit prize might argue for waiting.
uncertainties: Girvin and others in the original proposal are not credited.
Proximity to the 2025 prize might make the committee hesitate.
Credit between theory and experiment on the early papers is not fully settled in the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turned the no-cloning and measurement principles into a protocol whose security rests on physical law. It started a practical field of quantum communication and connected foundational quantum mechanics to technology. Originality is high, and the 2022 Bell-test prize and 2025 circuit prize set a context where this is a natural neighbour.
assessment.attribution: BB84 (Bennett and Brassard) is the foundational protocol; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is independent and linked to Bell tests. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a priority matter and is not credited here. The three-name configuration is plausible but the weight between BB84 and E91 is debated.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations, satellite links and commercial systems exist, so the idea is well confirmed in practice. Real-world security (device imperfections) is an ongoing issue but does not undermine the principle.
uncertainties: Wiesner's earlier work and the physics versus computer-science nature of the contribution may argue against a physics prize.
Attribution between BB84 and E91 is contestable.
Practical security of deployed systems is still partly open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models with tunable parameters, giving direct access to the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site imaging. It is a cornerstone of analogue quantum simulation and of atomic many-body physics, the area closest to my own field, so I note that I may judge it with more familiarity than other entries.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 Mott transition; Bloch and Greiner developed quantum-gas microscopes; Esslinger delivered the fermionic Mott insulator. The cap of three names forces leaving out Esslinger, and Jaksch is not credited. This makes the allocation hard and I put the weight on the foundational proposal and the experiments.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories and increasingly used to answer questions in condensed matter, although the simulator has not yet solved an open problem beyond classical computation in a decisive way. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is difficult and Jaksch is missing.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize on quantum systems.
The extent to which simulations have answered open physics questions is still limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos and the association with the blazar TXS 0506+056 and with the Galactic plane opened neutrino astronomy at TeV to PeV energies, a new window on cosmic-ray accelerators.
assessment.attribution: Halzen led the conception and the collaboration; Karle was involved in the detector construction and the science. Spiering is credited and I recognise his role in the field, but the collaboration is very large and credit cannot be reduced to two or three names without controversy. I propose Halzen and Karle on the supplied names, with real concern about fairness.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux has been confirmed in several channels and the source identifications are emerging but partial. The discovery is secure; the interpretation of sources is still developing, so timing is somewhat early to mid.
uncertainties: Large collaboration makes a fair two- or three-person allocation hard.
Source identification is still preliminary.
Overlap with the 2002 prize for cosmic neutrinos.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Event Horizon Telescope produced the first images of the shadow of the M87 black hole and later of Sagittarius A*, demonstrating horizon-scale imaging by very long baseline interferometry at 1.3 mm and giving direct strong-field tests. It is a technical and scientific achievement, and complements the 2020 black-hole prize.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept; Doeleman led the technical development of mm-VLBI and the collaboration; Zensus is the third credited name. The collaboration involves hundreds of people, so the choice of two or three is contentious. I propose Falcke and Doeleman while noting that this might not match the committee's view.
assessment.maturity: Two sources imaged with consistent results with general relativity, but the tests are limited in precision and polarisation results are still developing. Recognition is likely a bit early.
uncertainties: A very large collaboration makes allocation contentious.
The strength of the gravity tests is modest at present.
I am relying on memory of who proposed what.
